chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan (may Allah have mercy on him) narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Abu Abdillah al-Razi narrated to us, from Nasr ibn al-Sabah, from al-Mufaddal ibn Umar, who said: I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

and a man asked him: In what amount does the alms-tax (zakat) of wealth become obligatory? So he said to him: Do you intend the apparent alms-tax or the internal one? He said: I intend both of them. He said: As for the apparent, in every thousand there is twenty-five dirhams, and as for the internal, do not monopolize for yourself that which your brother is more in need of than you.

key_terms.تَسْتَأْثِرْ: To monopolize or keep for oneself exclusively
key_terms.خَمْسَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ دِرْهَمًا: Twenty-five dirhams (the specific amount for zakat per thousand)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between apparent and internal alms-tax in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Mani al-Akhbar*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates the dual dimensions of charity by distinguishing between *zakat al-zahir* (external alms-tax), quantified as 2.5% of wealth, and *zakat al-batin* (internal alms-tax), defined ethically as sharing surplus resources with those in greater need. This distinction highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on integrating legal obligation (*fard*) with spiritual refinement (*akhlaq*), where the latter transforms material wealth into a means of social solidarity and self-purification. The teaching underscores that true piety requires not only fulfilling the fixed financial duty but also cultivating a generous disposition that prioritizes the well-being of the community.
